title: Plan your retreat
hook: a day, a weekend or ten days: plan one for this coming year

segments.voice: Yesterday, the meal chant: not for fun, not for looks, only to keep this body going. Your line was for health, not vanity. Did you take one breath before the first bite? Day one thousand four hundred eleven.

Once, the Buddha told his monks that he wanted to go into seclusion for three months, and that no one should come to him except the one who brought his alms food. The monks agreed. Three months went by. When he came out, he told them how he had spent most of that time: mindful of the breath, in and out. The teacher of the whole community took time away. He planned it, he told people, and he came back and said what he did there. That's a retreat. Today, with the year's practice traditions nearly done, plan your retreat.
screen: `THE BUDDHA GOES INTO SECLUSION.` → `ONLY THE ONE WHO BRINGS FOOD.` → `HE COMES BACK AND TELLS THEM.`

segments.voice: That story is in the Connected Discourses, in the chapter on breathing. It gives a retreat its shape: a set time, a protected space, a plain practice, and a return. Retreat is woven through Buddhist life. The monks' rains retreat, the vassa, began in the Vinaya with a simple rule: during the rainy season, stay put in one place. Tradition makes that season a stretch of deeper practice, and lay people may join in, coming to the monastery on moon days. Earlier on this path, we visited sesshin, the Zen week of silence. And in some meditation centers today, people sit for ten days in silence. But a retreat doesn't have to be long. A day of mindfulness at home counts. So does a weekend at a monastery that welcomes guests. What makes it a retreat is not the length. It's the same four things from the Buddha's three months: a time you decide on in advance, a space protected from ordinary demands, one plain practice, and a way back. The planning is not a chore before the real thing. In the Buddha's story, telling the monks was part of it. Someone knew where he was and who would bring the food. If you've walked this path for a while, the practices of these past weeks, chanting, bowing, pilgrimage, the perfections, the moon days, all live more deeply on a retreat. So the task today is small and practical. Not go now. Write it down: when, where, how long, and who will know.
screen: `THE BUDDHA'S THREE MONTHS AWAY.` · `VASSA: STAY PUT FOR THE RAINS.` · `A DAY, A WEEKEND OR TEN DAYS.` · then, large: `WHEN, WHERE, HOW LONG, WHO KNOWS.`

segments.voice: Sit for a few breaths first, the way the Buddha spent his three months: just the breath, in and out. Then, if you'd like, let a plan take shape. When could you step away this coming year? A Saturday? A long weekend? Ten days? Where would you go: your own room with the phone off, a nearby temple, a center that runs retreats? What one practice would you keep there? And who would you tell? After the bell, write those four answers down, even in pencil. The bell holds the time.
Plan your retreat. A set time, a protected place, one plain practice and a way back, decided before you go, as the Buddha did. Today's word.
Your line: plan it. Today, put one possible retreat date on your calendar, and tell one person about it. Day one thousand four hundred eleven.

howItsDone: Buddhists go on retreats of a day, a weekend or longer at monasteries and meditation centers; monks keep the vassa, the rains retreat, and lay people may join it on observance days.

original.note: Pali vassa (Sanskrit varsha): the rains, and the rains retreat monks keep each year.

trapdoor: what you thought: a retreat is a long, expensive trip for serious meditators.
what it means: any set time, protected space, plain practice and a way back, planned in advance.
what a scholar hears: the Buddha's three months of breath meditation in the Samyutta Nikaya's chapter on breathing, and the vassa rule of the Vinaya.

notes: SN 54.11 paraphrased: the Buddha at Icchanangala wishes to go into seclusion for three months with no one approaching except the one bringing almsfood; afterward he says he dwelt mostly in concentration by mindfulness of breathing. Confirm 'three months' and 'most of that time'.
Vinaya Mahavagga III: rule to enter the rains residence; paraphrased as 'stay put in one place'. Confirm.
Lay people joining the vassa on moon days is general; confirm.
'Ten days in silence' at some meditation centers taken from the index; no organization named. Confirm.
